cells.tense: You are carrying real clarity into the group's practices right now.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Pick a shared practice that has gone thin and change one concrete part of how it runs — a small shift the others will notice without being told.
cells.core:
There is a practice you share with other people, and you are the one who can see what it actually does and what it has stopped doing. You bring method to it: you notice which part of the ritual has quietly stopped working, and you hold that knowledge steady without turning it into a fight. That kind of clarity is rare among groups, and it is what keeps a shared thing alive instead of merely repeated.

What this season wants is one real inch. Take a practice you share that has gone thin and change one concrete part of it — not a rewrite, not a speech, a small shift the others will feel. Insight that stays a private opinion changes nothing; make the move and the insight becomes something the group can stand on.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what a shared practice needs and change it.
cells.verb: Bringing disciplined inquiry and method into shared practices.
cells.place: Where a group's meaning lives in shared practice.

cells.tense: You are working out in advance how the whole shared practice ought to look.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Before the group's ritual meets again, set down a condition you held about how it must go, and carry in only what you truly need from it.
cells.core:
In the practices your group keeps, your method has begun moving faster than the group itself. You know how the gathering should go, how the tradition should look in a year, which parts are worn out — and the plan is fully built before anyone else has arrived. What the others get is a finished thing to agree with rather than a practice they helped make, and they have started holding back their own part of it.

The act here is release. Before the practice meets again, let go of a condition about how it has to unfold, and bring only the single need you actually have from it. Keep whatever is genuinely alive in the tradition; release the rest of the blueprint. The change you want is slower this way, and it holds.
cells.sheetLine: You have the whole thing built before anyone else arrives.
cells.verb: Bringing disciplined inquiry and method into shared practices.
cells.place: Where a group's meaning lives in shared practice.

cells.tense: You knew exactly what was wrong with the shared practice back then.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Put a plain name on how you feel about a shared practice that went off — no fixing, no explaining, just the name, and let that stand.
cells.core:
A practice you share with people still stands there in your mind, and you can describe precisely what was wrong with it — what had gone hollow, which part did not work. You stopped saying so, or you stopped going, and the analysis stays intact with nobody using it. What is missing is not the clarity; there is plenty of that. What has gone quiet is the plain, fair thing you feel about having stood in that practice.

Put it into words for yourself, honestly, without deciding yet what to do about it. That is the whole act: a fair call about a real feeling, nothing more. Your method is not the problem — what went quiet is the person the method belongs to, and saying how you feel is how the two come back into touch.
cells.sheetLine: You can still say what was wrong, and not what you felt.
cells.verb: Bringing disciplined inquiry and method into shared practices.
cells.place: Where a group's meaning lives in shared practice.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what your group will do next, and you would say you are only watching.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Picture a part of a shared practice as you would like it a year from now — loosely, while unsure — then take the small step that picture suggests.
cells.core:
Quietly, you are the one who decides what the group keeps and what it sets down. You would say you are just observing; you have a view. When a shared practice gets adjusted, your reading of what it should be is already present before decisions are made, and it is usually the reading that sticks — and no one has told you that you are the author of it.

The loosening here is not a bigger plan but a dreamed one. Picture a part of a shared practice as you would actually like it in a year, not as it should be, and feel your way toward it while staying unsure. Then take the small step that picture suggests. Knowing you are the one steering where the group heads is more honest than calling it observation.
cells.sheetLine: You say you are watching, and your view is deciding.
cells.verb: Bringing disciplined inquiry and method into shared practices.
cells.place: Where a group's meaning lives in shared practice.
